problems.description: test_app.py defines a class that violates PascalCase naming and module-level constants that are not UPPER_CASE
app.py wholesale rewrite (238/-240 lines) discards the previous seed structure in one commit; acceptable for a greenfield story session but means no incremental history for the old module

strengths: Single coherent async design: WebSocket and /health share one port with no framework dependency
SonarQube delta shows net improvement: 4 smells and 10 cognitive-complexity points removed, 0 new bugs, 0.0% duplications
Removes the previous hardcoded static-salt password hashing in favor of a cleaner message server
Clear module docstring explaining the architectural decision
commit_reviews.summary: A sound greenfield session that replaces the seed with a leaner, less complex async notification server while introducing only minor test-file naming violations.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +52 for a 164-line change: `_process_request` and the message-routing branch grew deeply nested conditionals (endpoint parsing, channel validation, per-type dispatch all inline). This should be decomposed into per-endpoint/per-message-type handlers to stay maintainable.

Dual channel resolution — `message.get("channel")` falling back to `payload.get("channel")` — creates two sources of truth for where a channel lives in the wire contract, making the protocol ambiguous for clients.

SonarQube reports +1 bug introduced by this commit. The exact location is not identifiable from the visible diff (likely the hand-rolled `/channels/{}/subscribers` path slicing or control-message handling); it warrants targeted review.

Brittle string-slicing URL parsing (`path[len("/channels/"):-len("/subscribers")]`) with `unquote` applied only to the channel segment while `urlsplit` handles the rest — inconsistent and fragile for encoded channel names.

Duplication +2.2%: the channel-membership gate (`channel is None or id in channel_subscribers(channel)`) is repeated across the direct and system message branches, and the channel-cleanup-on-remove logic mirrors the unsubscribe logic.
Two convention violations reported in test_app.py (Classes should use PascalCase; Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), which deviate from the repo's snake_case test-function style.

strengths: Channel state is encapsulated in the thread-safe ClientRegistry with defensive copies and cleanup on disconnect, matching the existing lock-based registry pattern
Backward-compatible wire format: the channel field is optional and only added to the message when present
Subscription acks reuse the existing system message type, keeping the message contract predictable
Broad validation of channel type/non-emptyness integrated with the existing invalid-message rejection path
Strong test coverage: 7 new async tests including backward compatibility, multi-channel, REST endpoints, and disconnect cleanup
Switching /health to urlsplit robustly handles query strings on the path
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-tested channel subscribe/unsubscribe feature that respects the existing registry/contract patterns but introduces significant handler complexity (+52 cognitive, +1 bug, 2.2% duplication) that should be refactored before it grows.

problems.description: client_id is taken verbatim from the WebSocket query string without validation, so any client can claim another client's ID; ClientRegistry.add will overwrite the existing registry entry, hijacking that client's connection/messages.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +39 in a single commit signals _process_request and _handle_connection grew heavily; the branch-laden request handler should be decomposed into per-endpoint handlers.
SQLite URL path is parsed via magic string slicing (value[10:], value[9:]) in MessageStore instead of using urlsplit/urllib.parse, which is fragile against URL-encoded or prefixed forms.

MessageStore is documented as 'shared by all server instances' but each instance owns its own RLock; concurrent writers rely solely on SQLite database-level locking, so the guard is per-instance only.
New test_app.py code violates project conventions (classes not PascalCase, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE) — matches the 2 reported violations and the 0.82 convention score.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: MessageStore (persistence), RedisBroker (pub/sub transport), and NotificationServer (routing) are isolated, single-responsibility classes.
Redis is optional and env-driven; the server degrades gracefully to local-only operation when REDIS_URL is unset.
Parameterized SQLite queries (no string interpolation), sqlite3.Row access, and bounded limit/offset clamping with proper 400 responses on malformed input.
Proper async lifecycle: lazy broker start, CancelledError propagation in _consume, and full teardown in stop()/close().
Respects existing patterns: ClientRegistry.add extended with an optional client_id default, type hints on public signatures, snake_case functions and PascalCase classes.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured integration commit that cleanly adds SQLite persistence and Redis pub/sub to the notification server with proper lifecycle handling and input validation, though it introduces modest technical debt via high cognitive complexity, unvalidated client_id spoofing, and test-side convention violations.

problems.description: Dual bookkeeping of connections: WebSocketTransport._connections and ClientRegistry both hold the same connection objects, so the abstraction is half-done — ClientRegistry remains the source of truth for presence checks while the transport owns delivery. The two maps must be kept in sync in on_connect/on_disconnect and could drift.

The new BaseTransport abstraction, WebSocketTransport, and TRANSPORTS registry have no accompanying tests; the diff touches only app.py. The transport selection path (env-driven, ValueError on unknown name) is untested.
SonarQube reports +1 new bug in this refactor that is not evident from manual review; the flagged defect should be inspected in the analyzer before merge.

The 2 flagged convention violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE module constant) are located in test_app.py, which this commit does not modify — they are pre-existing, not introduced here. The commit's own additions (BaseTransport, WebSocketTransport, TRANSPORTS) comply with the reported conventions.

strengths: Clean strategy/adapter extraction: BaseTransport ABC with a well-scoped interface and a TRANSPORTS registry keyed by env var, matching the codebase's dict-registry pattern.
Large cognitive-complexity reduction (-26) and smell reduction (-2); the broadcast path is simplified and deduplicated.
Transport is constructor-injectable, improving testability and enabling future non-WebSocket transports without touching notification logic.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive transport-abstraction refactor (-26 cognitive complexity, cleaner delivery interface) that slightly under-delivers because connections are still stored in two places, the new abstraction lacks tests, and the two reported convention violations live in an unmodified file (test_app.py) rather than in this commit.

problems.description: In-process fallback rate limiter (_rate_windows dict) grows unbounded with no eviction of stale client_ids; acceptable for now but leaks under many clients.
_cleanup_loop only handles CancelledError; any exception from _cleanup_messages/delete_older_than silently kills the background task with no logging.
MessageStore.history cursor uses strict 'timestamp > ?', so messages sharing the exact same timestamp as the cursor are skipped on the next page.
Mechanical measurement flags 2 convention violations in test_app.py (Classes should use PascalCase; module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE).
delete_older_than compares ISO timestamp strings lexicographically with no index hint; fine at current scale, could degrade as message table grows.

strengths: Clean rate-limiting seam: atomic Redis pipeline path with an in-process fallback when no broker is present, matching the existing broker-or-local pattern.
Background cleanup task lifecycle is properly managed — created in start(), cancelled and gathered in stop().
New /history endpoint and rate limit follow existing request-handler structure and are covered by added tests.
SonarQube delta shows improvement: -1 smell and -24 cognitive complexity, so the change reduces overall complexity.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-integrated feature commit that adds cursor-paginated history, TTL-based message cleanup, and dual-path rate limiting while respecting existing MessageStore/broker/server patterns, with only minor maintainability nits and the two measured test-file convention violations.

compounding_issues: Single-file monolith: all of app.py grows from 260 to ~560 LOC across the story (ClientRegistry, MessageStore, RedisBroker, transports, server, HTTP routes) with no module split, so later sessions had to thread new seams through one file

Hybrid sync/async design: ClientRegistry and MessageStore use threading.RLock/sqlite3 with check_same_thread=False inside an asyncio server, forcing session 5 to bolt an asyncio.Lock on top for the in-memory rate-limit fallback
Dual-mode rate limiting (Redis pipeline vs in-memory window) creates two code paths that can drift, and the in-memory fallback is per-process and resets on restart
Session 1's wholesale discard of the seed codebase means none of the seed's Flask/JWT/auth scaffolding carried forward (acceptable for greenfield, but the seed is effectively throwaway)
Repo hygiene: __pycache__ .pyc artifacts and the full .instrument/session.jsonl are committed in every session
key_decisions: Session 1: framework-free architecture — raw websockets asyncio server handling both WS upgrade and the /health HTTP response on one TCP port, replacing the Flask seed entirely; this set the whole design
Session 2: in-process channel registry (thread-safe dict in ClientRegistry) as the pub/sub model, which later forced the Redis broker and shaped session 5's rate limiting
Session 3: Redis as an optional external broker with in-memory fallback plus SQLite MessageStore persistence — the dual-mode decision that carried forward
Session 4: extracting BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport behind an abstract interface with a TRANSPORTS registry and TRANSPORT env selection, keeping the protocol layer transport-independent
Session 5: Redis-window atomic rate limiting (incr + 61s expiry) with in-memory fallback, plus TTL-based message retention enforced by a background hourly cleanup loop
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 built a clean, dependency-light core (4 tests); session 2 layered channels onto it cleanly (6 tests); session 3 integrated Redis and SQLite persistence (8 tests); session 4 was a disciplined, behavior-preserving refactor that introduced the transport abstraction while keeping all 8 tests green and public APIs intact; session 5 capped it with production cross-cutting concerns — rate limiting, message history, and TTL retention (10 tests). Every session ended with its full test suite passing, and the refactor-before-final-feature ordering shows deliberate technical-debt management rather than accumulation.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent story arc — core → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting — where each session builds directly on its predecessor with green tests throughout and quality improves to the end.
